questions.q: According to this lesson, why does clicking through a console stop working well once you're managing dozens of resources instead of one or two?
options: The console was built for a human making one careful decision at a time, not for repeating an identical decision across many resources
The console has a hard technical limit of five resources per subscription
Consoles are being deprecated by every major cloud provider
Automation is always required by cloud provider terms of service
questions.explain: The console works fine for a single resource, but it was never designed for repeating the same decision across dozens or hundreds of resources.

questions.q: What does it mean for manual console work to be 'not repeatable'?
options: There's no saved record of the exact steps taken, so doing it again means reconstructing it from memory
The console physically prevents you from creating the same resource twice
It means the work can only be done once per day
It refers to resources that cannot be deleted
questions.explain: Without a saved script, there's nothing to rerun — you're relying on memory to reproduce what you did.

questions.q: In the lesson's VM provisioning example, why is a script that loops once to create 50 VMs better than clicking through the console 50 times?
options: It produces VMs that are provably identical, since the exact same code ran for each one
It is the only method that works for more than 10 VMs
It automatically reduces the cost of each VM
It eliminates the need for a resource group
questions.explain: Each manual click is a separate chance for a setting to drift; a single script run applies identical logic to every VM.

questions.q: Why does tagging every resource in a subscription by hand through the portal tend to miss resources?
options: It relies on a person clicking through every resource individually, and large subscriptions make that easy to miss some
The portal doesn't support tags at all
Tags can only be applied to virtual machines, not other resource types
Resource tags expire automatically after 24 hours
questions.explain: A script that pulls the full resource list and loops through it touches every resource the list returns; manual clicking depends on a person not missing any.

questions.q: What is the real risk the lesson describes with manually rotating credentials across dozens of storage accounts?
options: Opening each account by hand and updating every place a key is used creates many chances to miss one or get the order wrong
Credentials cannot be rotated more than once per account
Rotating credentials manually is always faster than scripting it
Storage accounts don't support access key rotation
questions.explain: A script that loops through the account list performs the same rotation steps on every account, which is both faster and less likely to leave one on a stale key.
